Speculating About the Past - A Review

You can use could have to speculate about past events. Specifically, you use it to speculate about scenarios different from what actually occurred.
May have and might have can be used to speculate about the past.
You can also use would have and didn't need to to speculate.

You use could have in the following situations:

  1. to express past possibility
For example: He could have been a doctor if he had applied himself in school.

1. to express past uncertainty
For example: I'm not really sure who called. It could have been Rob, I guess.

You use may have to express past uncertainty.
For example: I suppose I may have been a bit tough on her.

You use might have to refer to a past possibility which did not occur.
For example: My goodness, you might have lost everything!

You use would have to express events that did not actually happen.
For example: I would have called you, but I didn't want to use up any more minutes on my cell.

You use didn't need to to express an unnecessary action that was not actually done.
For example: My computer was a bit slow, but fortunately it didn't need to be replaced.

There are two types of relative clauses: defining and non-defining.
Defining relative clauses give essential information to define or identify the person or thing we are talking about.
Non-defining relative clauses tell us more about someone or something, but the information in these clauses does not help us to define what we are talking about.
In defining relative clauses, you often omit the relative pronoun when it is the subject of the clause.
The excuse he offered was unconvincing. (that/which is omitted)

images.text: I have been a scuba diver most of my life. Scuba diving, a wonderful way to explore the deep mysteries of the ocean, was also a way of assisting investigators to find the cause of plane crashes and sea accidents. That was my day job. We helped the investigators recover the sunken remains of a shipwreck or  plane accident.  We, the divers, uncovered those important pieces of evidence helping to determine the cause of the disaster. Our underwater searches had to cover a wide range of territory and we often worked around the clock. The accident might have happened because of a mechanical failure, human error or mother nature's wrath.

The searches would have been slow due to bad weather. Also, the items we recovered might have needed to be lifted carefully with special equipment. We saw that the debris, waterlogged and heavy, might have easily broken apart, and it was always better to remove an item intact. I might have chosen a different career in another field but I loved diving. I didn't need to have outside hobbies because I was contented.

One wreckage we discovered during an investigation of a plane crash was fascinating. The ship was old and contained cargo — real treasure including gold bars and jewels. It might have been from the early 1800s but that wasn't easy to ascertain. The hull was so disintegrated that it was impossible to tell the type of boat it had been. Much to my disappointment the authorities kept the gold bars and jewelry. That was the only time I might have taken a souvenir, but I did not. The remnants of that ship are safely locked away until their origin can be established.
